eigen.note: When you were asked directly, you gave the full reason in the right order: kernel, then not invertible, then determinant zero. Unprompted you leave that reason out: in the closing summary and again in this review. The sign slip on the eigenvector came back in this review exactly as in your first lesson on $E_2$ of $\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$: a row with both coefficients positive, read off without the minus sign.

review.prompt: Give a $2 \times 2$ matrix with distinct real eigenvalues and nonzero off-diagonal entries (fresh numbers), chosen so that one eigenvalue's row $ax + by = 0$ has $a$ and $b$ of the same sign. Ask for that eigenspace with the reasoning, then why the eigenvalues are the roots of $\det(M - \lambda I)$.
points: Eigenvalues are the roots of $\det(M - \lambda I)$, here $\lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr} M)\lambda + \det M$
Why: an eigenvector is a nonzero $v$ in $\ker(M - \lambda I)$, so $M - \lambda I$ is not invertible and its determinant is $0$
The diagonal entries are not the eigenvalues when off-diagonal entries are nonzero
$E_\lambda$ is $\ker(M - \lambda I)$, a line for a $2 \times 2$ matrix with distinct eigenvalues
The vector read off the row is checked by substituting it back (sign check)

notation.text: The notes write vectors as columns and use $A^T$ for the transpose. They say ker and im, never null space. The eigenspace for an eigenvalue $\lambda$ is written $E_\lambda$ and is the kernel $\ker(A - \lambda I)$.

in-the-binomial-probability-binom-n-k-p-.text: In the binomial probability $\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$, the factor $(1-p)^{n-k}$ is called the **failure factor**. Its exponent is $n-k$, not $n$.

poisson-lesson.title: Poisson distribution lesson
poisson-lesson.goal: Understand where the Poisson formula $P(X=k) = e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}$ comes from as a limit of the binomial, and use it
poisson-lesson.step: Answer the open question on the failure factor in the binomial
poisson-lesson.help: You were told that the Poisson formula is the limit of a binomial over $n$ tiny slots with $p = 3/n$. You were told that $\left(1-\frac{3}{n}\right)^n \to e^{-3}$, not $1$, because the number of factors grows with $n$. You were told that the failure factor $\left(1-\frac{3}{n}\right)^{n-2}$ has exponent $n-2$, not $n$, so the known limit does not apply to it as written.
poisson-lesson.note: Plan map: exp-limit-shift then binomial-limit. Ask the check on $(1-3/n)^{n-2}$ again as it was (unanswered, answer never shown), then derive $\binom{n}{k}(\lambda/n)^k \to \lambda^k/k!$ and assemble the PMF; then use and contrast with binomial.
